abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a fundamental re-conceptualization of transport layer congestion control through a continuous-time dynamical systems framework, departing from the traditional discrete-time window-based paradigm that has dominated computer networks for decades. Current approaches rely on discrete packet acknowledgments and AIMD window updates, which introduce inherent oscillations and inefficiencies, particularly in high-bandwidth-delay-product networks. We propose a novel rate-based congestion control mechanism modeled as a coupled system of ordinary differential equations describing sender rates and queue evolution. The theoretical analysis leverages Lyapunov stability theory and contraction mapping principles to establish global convergence guarantees under general network conditions. Our mathematical framework reveals fundamental performance limitations inherent in discrete-time controllers and demonstrates that continuous-time regulation achieves strictly superior convergence rates. The analysis extends to multi-path scenarios where flow splitting dynamics exhibit emergent synchronization properties. Numerical experiments on ns-3 simulation validate the theoretical predictions, showing 40% improvement in convergence speed and 25% reduction in throughput oscillation compared to TCP CUBIC under emulated satellite link conditions. This work establishes a rigorous theoretical foundation for next-generation congestion control protocols that transcend the prevalent window-based paradigm.

This paper develops an enhanced theoretical framework for online traffic engineering in large-scale IP networks, addressing the fundamental tension between computational tractability and solution quality in real-time routing optimization. Existing theoretical models for traffic engineering rely on offline optimization or simplified fluid approximations that fail to capture the discrete nature of router forwarding tables and the dynamic characteristics of traffic matrices. We formulate a stochastic optimization problem that explicitly accounts for traffic demand uncertainty and routing table size constraints. The key theoretical contribution is a novel online learning algorithm with provably bounded regret, achieved through a carefully constructed decomposition of the routing space into equivalence classes. Our analysis demonstrates that the algorithm achieves O(√T) regret compared to the optimal offline routing configuration, representing a significant improvement over prior work that achieved O(T^(2/3)) bounds. The theoretical framework also provides precise conditions under which the algorithm approaches optimal performance, characterizing the inherent complexity of traffic engineering as a function of network topology and traffic variability. Simulation results on real backbone network topologies validate the theoretical findings and demonstrate substantial improvements in flow allocation efficiency under realistic traffic scenarios.

We present Orchestra, a completely redesigned network architecture for data center networks that eliminates the traditional separation between network state distribution and packet forwarding. Contemporary software-defined networking architectures suffer from inherent latency in control plane communication, where switch-level forwarding decisions must occasionally consult remote controllers, creating consistency challenges and performance bottlenecks. Orchestra fundamentally reimagines this architecture through a distributed state machine paradigm where network topology, reachability, and quality-of-service state is encoded directly in packet headers and processed at line rate by commodity switching hardware. The system introduces novel header fields that carry transitive, cryptographically authenticated assertions about network state, enabling switches to make locally optimal forwarding decisions that are globally consistent. We designed a complete protocol stack including state propagation mechanisms, conflict resolution procedures, and security extensions that protect against header spoofing and route manipulation attacks. Implementation on FPGA-based programmable switches demonstrates line-rate processing at 100 Gbps with nanosecond-scale state lookup latency. Evaluation in a 64-server testbed shows 99.9th percentile flow completion time reductions of 60% compared to OpenFlow-based SDN, while eliminating single points of failure inherent in centralized control planes. Orchestra opens new research directions for fully distributed, self-consistent network architectures.

This paper presents Chainlink, an enhanced network function virtualization platform that significantly advances the state of the art in service function chaining performance and elasticity. Existing NFV systems deploy service functions as isolated virtual machines or containers, resulting in substantial overhead from packet serialization, context switching, and inter-VM communication, particularly when service chains span multiple physical hosts. Chainlink addresses these inefficiencies through a novel co-design of the virtual switch data plane and service function placement. We introduce a lightweight interception mechanism that redirects traffic to in-host service functions without full packet encapsulation, achieving near-native forwarding performance. The system incorporates a distributed control plane that coordinates service function placement based on real-time load measurements and latency requirements, dynamically migrating functions to balance load while maintaining service chain integrity. We implemented Chainlink extensions for Open vSwitch and evaluated performance using a production-mixed workload trace. Results demonstrate 45% improvement in per-packet processing latency and 3.2× throughput gains compared to state-of-the-art approaches, while achieving 35% reduction in host-to-host chain migrations during traffic spikes. The design includes comprehensive security mechanisms ensuring chain integrity and flow-level isolation, validated through penetration testing against emulated attack scenarios.
